strengths: Addresses a practical bottleneck in video anomaly detection: the scarcity and cost of real abnormal videos. PA-VAD reframes training as generation-driven, using real normal videos plus synthesized pseudo-abnormal videos and evaluating on standard benchmarks.

The proposed CA-PAG is reasonably designed: CLIP-based class-relevant initial image selection and VLM-based prompt refinement improve the fidelity and scene consistency of generated pseudo anomalies, supported by FVD/KVD/FID/KID improvements and qualitative examples.

DARM identifies a credible failure mode of diffusion-generated anomalies—inflated spatiotemporal feature magnitude inducing MIL bias—and proposes domain alignment plus usage-aware memory updates. Ablation studies isolate the benefit of the update mechanism and the full DARM module.

The empirical results are strong on ShanghaiTech (98.2% AUC) and competitive on UCF-Crime (82.5% AUC). The paper includes extensive ablations, qualitative detection traces, generation-quality metrics, and computational-cost discussion.

The manuscript is generally clear, with informative figures, equations, and a supplementary section covering implementation details, prompts, and hyperparameters. Limitations are partially acknowledged.
weaknesses: The supervision claim needs clarification. The method trains without real abnormal videos, but it still uses abnormal class names to guide synthesis, so comparisons to unsupervised VAD methods under the same constraint are not fully fair. The claim that UVAD operates under exactly the same constraint is misleading because UVAD does not use abnormal class metadata.

The method requires knowledge of the abnormal class set at training/inference time and is evaluated only in closed-set settings. Generalization to unseen or open-ended anomaly categories is not tested; this is a significant limitation for practical deployment and undercuts the broad 'scalable deployment' claim.

No comparison is made to simpler or alternative pseudo-anomaly generation strategies (e.g., rule-based edits, inpainting, copy-paste, or other generative priors) under the same detector. Thus the specific contribution of CA-PAG and the diffusion model is not fully isolated from the benefit of additional class semantics or the priors of large pre-trained models.

Experimental evidence is limited to two datasets and appears to be single-run without error bars or statistical significance tests; no cross-dataset evaluation is provided. On UCF-Crime, PA-VAD still trails real-abnormal WVAD methods (82.5 vs. 87.0), and the paper does not deeply analyze why long-horizon anomalies remain difficult.

Some methodological details are underspecified, especially the detection feature extractor/backbone. The role of Qwen2.5-VL projector embeddings versus I3D features is unclear, as is the temporal alignment between 81-frame generated pseudo videos and real video segments. Reproducibility would benefit from code/data release.

The paper lacks discussion of societal impact and privacy risks associated with surveillance anomaly detection. It also does not thoroughly analyze failure modes beyond a few qualitative examples, despite using synthesized anomalies that may be detected from generation artifacts rather than genuine abnormal semantics.

strengths: The paper tackles a meaningful bottleneck in video anomaly detection: collecting real abnormal footage is costly, privacy-sensitive, and scarce. Replacing real abnormality supervision with generated pseudo-abnormal videos is a promising direction with practical relevance.

The proposed CA-PAG is a sensible and well-motivated pipeline: it uses CLIP-based class-aware initial image selection and VLM-based prompt refinement before video diffusion, improving the fidelity and scene consistency of synthesized pseudo anomalies over naive prompting.

The Domain-Aligned Regularized Module (DARM) is technically well-motivated. It explicitly addresses the feature-magnitude bias caused by generated pseudo anomalies and combines domain alignment with usage-aware memory updates. Ablation studies support the effectiveness of these components.

The empirical results are strong within the proposed Real/Pseudo setting: PA-VAD reaches 98.2% AUC on ShanghaiTech and 82.5% on UCF-Crime, outperforming UVAD baselines without real abnormal videos. The paper also includes generation-quality metrics, qualitative detection curves, and ablation studies on synthetic data amount.

The manuscript is generally clearly written, with a detailed supplement covering generation prompts, hyperparameters, computational cost, and implementation details. The limitations section is forthcoming about UCF-Crime underperformance and failure cases such as shoplifting.
weaknesses: The comparison to UVAD is not entirely apples-to-apples: PA-VAD uses abnormal class names to synthesize class-aware pseudo anomalies, whereas typical UVAD methods do not have access to anomaly class labels. This extra supervision may partly explain the gains and should be controlled or discussed more explicitly.

The method assumes anomaly class names are known at training time. This is a nontrivial assumption for open-world deployment, where abnormal events may be unknown, compositional, or differently named across domains. The paper does not sufficiently analyze robustness when class names are absent, noisy, or incomplete.

The title 'Pseudo Anomalies Are All You Need' overstates the contribution: the approach still relies on real normal videos, anomaly class metadata, large pretrained vision-language models, and a powerful video diffusion model. It also does not surpass real-abnormal WVAD methods on UCF-Crime, which is acknowledged but weakens the strongest possible claim.

The generation cost is substantial: the supplement reports roughly 30 hours for ShanghaiTech and 55 hours for UCF-Crime on a high-memory GPU. While the paper notes this, the practical scalability claim would be stronger with a more thorough cost-benefit analysis or cheaper generation alternatives.

Evaluation is limited to two datasets. Cross-dataset generalization, open-set anomaly detection, and more challenging benchmarks such as XD-Violence are not explored. It is unclear whether the observed gains would transfer to longer, more complex, or differently distributed surveillance domains.

The contribution of prompt refinement appears modest in the ablation once DARM is enabled, and the overall performance depends heavily on the usage-aware memory update. The paper could better disentangle the separate effects of more supervision (class names), generation quality, and DARM regularization.

strengths: Targets a practical and important problem: reducing reliance on scarce and expensive real abnormal videos for weakly supervised video anomaly detection.
Introduces a complete pipeline (PA-VAD) combining class-aware initial image selection, VLM-based prompt refinement, and image-to-video diffusion for pseudo-anomaly generation.
Proposes DARM to address the feature-norm magnitude bias of generated pseudo anomalies and stabilize MIL training, with ablations isolating its components.
Reports strong frame-level AUC on ShanghaiTech (98.2%) and competitive performance on UCF-Crime, suggesting pseudo-only training can work in some settings.
The supplement provides useful implementation details, hyperparameters, and a candid discussion of generation cost.
weaknesses: Unfair experimental comparisons and unclear supervision level: PA-VAD uses abnormal class names, a VLM, and a large video diffusion model, while UVAD baselines are truly unsupervised and WWAD baselines use real abnormal videos; the paper does not compare under an equivalent supervision setting, so claims of outperforming both families are not substantiated.
The 'unsupervised training regime' claim is misleading: abnormal class names are provided and used to condition generation, which is additional supervisory information unavailable to UVAD methods.

Potential pretraining data contamination is not discussed: Wan2.2 and Qwen3-30B are pretrained on large-scale web data and may have seen UCF-Crime/ShanghaiTech or similar surveillance anomalies, which undermines the 'no real abnormal videos' claim.
The title and framing overstate the contribution: the method still requires real normal videos, abnormal class names, CLIP, a VLM, a huge video diffusion model, and substantial compute.

Novelty is incremental: the framework largely combines existing components (CLIP retrieval, VLM prompting, diffusion-based video generation, memory-based MIL, DANN domain alignment) with limited new technical insight.
Computational cost is very high: roughly 95 GB GPU memory and 30-55 hours of generation per dataset, which weakens the practical scalability argument.
Generation-quality evaluation lacks external baselines and human assessment; Table 3 only compares 'w/o Refine' vs. 'w/ Refine', so the quality claim is weak.

DARM's domain-alignment objective is somewhat confusing: it aligns real Normal and pseudo-Normal distributions, but the main failure mode it targets (magnitude bias of pseudo-abnormal clips) is not directly aligned with real abnormal data.
Baseline coverage is limited; recent weakly supervised VAD methods are omitted, and the table mixes protocols without fully clarifying whether comparisons are like-for-like.
Limitations are acknowledged only briefly; failure cases and when synthetic pseudo anomalies hurt performance are not adequately analyzed.
Reproducibility and data provenance are insufficiently addressed: code release, contamination checks, and details of pretrained model training data are not described.

strengths: The paper presents a practical pseudo-only VAD pipeline that eliminates the need for real abnormal training videos by using diffusion-generated pseudo anomalies from normal images.
It identifies a specific pseudo-induced magnitude bias in MIL training and proposes DARM to mitigate it; ablation studies show clear gains from both domain alignment and usage-aware memory updates.

Experiments are extensive across ShanghaiTech, UCF-Crime, and XD-Violence, including generation-quality metrics, open-set evaluation, ablations, and computational cost; results show strong AUC improvements over several UVAD baselines.
The method is well motivated and reproducible: hyperparameters, prompts, generation settings, and training details are largely provided, and limitations are explicitly discussed.
weaknesses: The training regime uses abnormal class names in addition to normal videos, which is extra semantic supervision not available in standard UVAD. This makes comparison to UVAD methods unfair and the description of the regime as 'unsupervised' misleading; the method should be framed as class-aware or evaluated against methods with equivalent side information.

DARM largely combines existing components (DANN-style domain alignment and memory updates) with limited theoretical analysis. The magnitude-bias analysis is mostly empirical and the huge norm inflation seen in Table 5b is not fully explained; it could be an artifact of MIL/top-k training rather than a general property of pseudo anomalies.

On UCF-Crime, the method remains below strong WWAD methods that use real abnormal videos, and the paper acknowledges that long, context-heavy anomalies are difficult to synthesize. The claim of matching or exceeding real/real pipelines is therefore only partially supported and dataset-dependent.

The framework depends on large pretrained VLM and diffusion models, involves substantial generation cost (roughly 30-55 GPU hours per dataset), and may inherit biases from these models. Generalization to truly unseen anomaly classes when no class names are available remains unclear.

Comparisons with prior pseudo-anomaly generation methods are limited to a few baselines and mainly on SHT/Crime, lacking broader evaluation on XD-Violence. Some reproducibility details, such as the full VLM instruction prompt being in Chinese, may also limit accessibility.

strengths: Introduces a pseudo-only VAD training pipeline that eliminates the need for real abnormal videos by synthesizing class-aware pseudo anomalies from only normal images and class text, reducing data collection and privacy constraints.

Identifies a concrete failure mode—pseudo-induced spatiotemporal magnitude bias—and proposes DARM with domain alignment and usage-aware memory updates; ablations and norm analyses provide evidence for both components and the bias-mitigation mechanism.

Extensive experiments across ShanghaiTech, UCF-Crime, and XD-Violence, including generation-quality metrics, frame-level AUC comparisons, open-set evaluations, qualitative detection traces, and ablations, which support the main claims.

Achieves strong results, including 98.2% AUC on ShanghaiTech and 95.1% on XD-Violence, outperforming the compared UVAD baselines and some real-abnormal WWAD methods in those settings, demonstrating that pseudo-only VAD can be competitive.
The paper is clearly organized and written, with limitations discussed, and the supplementary material provides useful generation and training details for reproducibility.
The Class-Aware Pseudo-Anomaly Generator with CLIP-based initial image selection and VLM prompt refinement improves generation fidelity, as shown by FVD/KVD gains and qualitative examples.
weaknesses: The pseudo-only setup still relies on very large pretrained diffusion and vision-language models (Wan2.2, Qwen2.5-VL, CLIP), which may encode prior semantic knowledge and introduce substantial compute requirements (e.g., roughly 30–55 GPU hours per dataset on two RTX 6000 Ada GPUs), complicating claims of data-free efficiency and fair comparison to simpler baselines.

On UCF-Crime, PA-VAD (82.5% AUC) underperforms strong real/real WWAD methods such as UR-DMU (87.0%) and MGSTRL (87.5%), so the broad claim that high-accuracy VAD is attainable without real abnormal videos is not fully supported for long, context-heavy anomalies.

DARM combines existing ideas—domain-adversarial alignment, UR-DMU memory banks, and usage-aware prototype updates—so the algorithmic novelty is moderate; the theoretical justification for why usage-aware updates specifically correct MIL magnitude bias is primarily empirical rather than formally established.

The method uses abnormal class names during pseudo-anomaly generation/training, which is a form of weak supervision; comparisons to UVAD methods that never see abnormal labels may not be strictly apples-to-apples, and the supervision access should be clearly matched or discussed.

Different feature backbones are used across compared methods (e.g., Qwen2.5-VL for PA-VAD versus 3D or CLIP features for others), which may confound reported gains; controlled comparisons with the same feature extractor would strengthen the empirical claims.

Some implementation choices—especially VLM prompt engineering and the initial image retrieval details—are deferred to the supplementary and rely on specific prompt wording, which may limit reproducibility without code and exact prompt/model release.

strengths: Addresses an important and practical problem: video anomaly detection without real abnormal videos, which can reduce reliance on scarce or privacy-sensitive abnormal footage.
Provides a clear pipeline that combines CLIP-based initial image selection, VLM-based prompt refinement, and image-to-video diffusion for class-aware pseudo-anomaly generation.
Identifies and mitigates the pseudo-induced feature magnitude bias with DARM; the feature-norm analysis (Tables 1 and 5b) supports the motivation.

Reports extensive experiments on ShanghaiTech, UCF-Crime, and XD-Violence, including ablations, open-set evaluations, and comparisons with UVAD, WVAD, and pseudo-data methods, with strong results on SHT and XD-Violence.
weaknesses: The comparison with prior methods may be confounded by feature extractor choice: PA-VAD uses a much stronger Qwen2.5-VL backbone while several baselines use I3D/C3D, so gains cannot be attributed solely to pseudo-anomaly generation and DARM.

The claimed practical advantage of avoiding real abnormal data is weakened by reliance on very large pretrained diffusion and VLM models and by high synthesis cost (e.g., up to 55 GPU-hours on two RTX 6000 Ada GPUs for UCF-Crime).

The method is not strictly unsupervised because it uses abnormal class names and large pretrained vision-language priors at training time, making the comparison with UVAD settings less direct than implied.

Long-duration, context-heavy anomalies such as shoplifting remain poorly synthesized, and performance on UCF-Crime is substantially below the best WVAD and SF-VAD/FPL results, limiting the generality of the pseudo-only claim.

Key ablations for DARM are mostly on ShanghaiTech; full component ablations on UCF-Crime and XD-Violence are missing, so the separate importance of domain alignment and usage-aware memory updates is not fully established across datasets.

Novelty is incremental: DARM combines existing DANN and memory-usage mechanisms, while the generation pipeline composes off-the-shelf CLIP, VLM, and I2V diffusion models; reproducibility details and code release are also not clearly provided.
